unit: one fixed residual-state workload profile (eight per suite: each of four fact slices under two profiles) with its fact-table slice of real, unique Corporacion Favorita sales rows (1.03 to 2.14 million rows; development slices dated 2017-02-02 to 2017-04-30, graded slices 2017-05-01 to 2017-07-30), tree depth, estimator count, learning rate, and normalized join topology

metrics.name: elapsed_seconds
metrics.means: the median complete-fit wall time over the workload's four interleaved paired repetitions, each a fresh benchmark process; the interval includes model.fit and fitted-model validation and ends before the private joined table is registered
metrics.source: judge/benchmark.py measures time.perf_counter around GradientBoosting.fit plus _validate_fitted_model; judge/evaluator.py _run_paired runs, for each of four repetitions and each workload, one fresh reference and one fresh candidate benchmark process back to back in the pre-recorded alternation PAIR_ORDER (reference first, candidate first, reference first, candidate first; repetitions outer, workloads inner), and _summarize takes the median of the four samples independently for candidate and reference
metrics.clears_when: the candidate passes the existing RMSE and sorted-prediction L1 validity bounds on every repetition for workload w and candidate_elapsed_seconds(w) < reference_elapsed_seconds(w), each the median of that implementation's four paired repetitions

metrics.name: residual_update_seconds
metrics.means: the paper's residual update time (JoinBoost, PVLDB 16, Section 5.3/5.4, Fig. 5 'Residual update time' and the update bars of Fig. 14): total wall time spent in GradientBoosting._update_error, the between-round residual-state advance, summed over every boosting round of one complete fit, each round including one trusted full read of the updated target state before the clock stops. Per workload, the median over the same four interleaved paired repetitions that define elapsed_seconds, taken independently of elapsed
metrics.source: judge/benchmark.py wraps GradientBoosting._update_error at class level (timed_update_error) with a time.perf_counter bound before any candidate import; the fixed GradientBoosting.train_one (fingerprint-protected) calls it once per tree. Inside the clock, after the submitted method returns, the wrapper reads the residual column of the target relation of the state the next tree will consume (the returned state's, else model.cjt's) on the judge's own connection; a relation that is not a table is first computed in full into a temporary table and discarded. The sum of squared residuals read must equal the value before the update minus (2*lr - lr^2) * sum_leaf(g^2/h) to a relative 1e-6 and the relation must hold every fact row. The value is reported only if the call count equals n_estimators, the timed class attribute was neither replaced nor shadowed on the instance, and every trusted read was consistent; otherwise it is unmeasured (null). judge/evaluator.py _run_paired runs, for each of four repetitions and each workload, one fresh reference and one fresh candidate benchmark process back to back in the pre-recorded alternation PAIR_ORDER (reference first, candidate first, reference first, candidate first; repetitions outer, workloads inner), and _summarize takes the median of the four update samples (unmeasured if any sample is) independently for candidate and reference; _workload_decisions compares the medians
metrics.clears_when: the candidate passes the existing RMSE and sorted-prediction L1 validity bounds on every repetition for workload w, both update times are measured, and candidate_residual_update_seconds(w) < reference_residual_update_seconds(w), each the median of that implementation's four paired repetitions
metrics.tolerance: none; equality fails, the same rule as elapsed_seconds

metrics.name: rmse_error
metrics.means: the paper's model-accuracy axis (JoinBoost Fig. 8c, Section 6.1: JoinBoost and LightGBM have equivalent rmse because they run the same algorithm): absolute difference between the fitted model's training RMSE over the private materialized join and the materialized-join scikit-learn oracle's RMSE, maximized over the workload's four repetitions
metrics.source: judge/benchmark.py computes abs(candidate_rmse - oracle_rmse) after the timed interval from model.compute_rmse on the private joined table and GradientBoostingRegressor on the same rows; judge/evaluator.py _summarize keeps the maximum over repetitions
metrics.clears_when: candidate_rmse_error(w) <= 1e-3 on every repetition of workload w (accuracy equivalence with the oracle). The reference must satisfy the same bound and the prediction L1 bound on every repetition; otherwise the verification fails as a reference failure
metrics.tolerance: the existing absolute 1e-3 equivalence bound, unchanged from the validity gate; no reference-relative numerical tolerance is invented

beats_reference: beats_reference = 1 if and only if all eight selected workloads pass all three metrics: elapsed_seconds, residual_update_seconds and rmse_error. Both timing metrics compare medians of four interleaved paired repetitions run in a fixed pre-recorded alternation order. A candidate must also satisfy the existing model-structure gates, the trusted-executor rules (scalar result types only; rows, columns, values and bytes returned to Python bounded per query and per fit; allowed statements; unmodified executor), the non-materialised-join rule (no relation with at least 10% of the fact rows may carry more than 4 columns beyond the fact table's own; checked after every boosting round and at the end of the fit) and, on every repetition of every workload, rmse_error <= 1e-3 and prediction_l1 <= rows * 1e-6. One failed workload or metric makes the overall verdict fail; aggregate elapsed, aggregate continuous score, and improvements on other workloads or metrics cannot compensate. A reference that cannot be prepared, fails, times out, violates the RMSE or prediction-L1 bounds, or lacks a trusted update clock, and a failed bundled baseline, are failed verifications raised to the verifier adapter, never a bar and never a candidate score.
statement_sentences: A separate beats-reference verdict accompanies the continuous score. It requires the candidate to satisfy every existing model and numerical validity gate and, independently on each of the eight selected workloads, to have a strictly lower median complete-fit time and a strictly lower median residual update time (total time inside GradientBoosting._update_error across all boosting rounds) than the optimized reference, each over four repetitions in which fresh candidate and reference processes alternate in a fixed pre-recorded order, and an RMSE within 1e-3 of the materialized-join oracle on every repetition. Equality or a loss on any workload or metric fails the overall verdict, even if the summed runtime or continuous score improves. Reference measurements, workload identities attached to decisions, and final-suite measurements remain private; development feedback exposes only per-metric pass/fail counts and percentages.
comments: M087 replaces the historical aggregate-score comparator for this T40 task. Elapsed complete-fit time is the task's existing reference-relative performance objective. RMSE error and sorted-prediction L1 retain their existing absolute 1e-3 per-repetition validity gates; the protected source contains no approved reference-relative numerical-error tolerance, so this specification does not invent one. The separately authorized continuous score uses the fixed bundled per-leaf baseline: L=max(0,log10(B/T)) and score=100*L/(2+L), with no finite upper clipping. Changing the optimized PASS reference cannot change that score. Workload profiles, seeds, repetitions, timing interval, baseline, reference, and PASS relation are unchanged. BEAT SPEC V2 (2026-10-07): adds residual_update_seconds, the paper's residual update time for the selected between-round update contribution (Section 5.3/5.4, Figs. 5 and 14), measured in the same timed fits by a trusted class-level wrapper around the fixed train_one -> _update_error call site, with the same strict per-workload rule; and rmse_error, the paper's accuracy-equivalence axis (Fig. 8c), as an explicit per-workload metric using the unchanged absolute 1e-3 oracle bound. Both are conjoined with the unchanged elapsed_seconds rule. A failed or untrusted update clock leaves residual_update_seconds unmeasured (metric fails) rather than invalidating the fit, so validity and the continuous score are unchanged. Residual limitation: work deferred out of _update_error into later tree growth is not counted as update time but still counts in the conjoined complete-fit time. Not added: Fig. 14 train-only time (complete-fit time already covers it, and a strict comparison on an unchanged phase would be decided by noise), Fig. 9 query counts (diagnostic, inside editable code), memory and multi-node/out-of-core scalability (LightGBM out-of-memory comparisons need data sizes and machines beyond this task), and comparisons with LightGBM/XGBoost/LMFAO/MADLib (other systems, not the reference). Reference validity: the reference is now checked against the RMSE and prediction-L1 bounds on every repetition, and reference or baseline failures raise a failed verification instead of a zero candidate score. Workload profiles, seeds, repetitions, timing interval, baseline, reference and continuous score are unchanged. PAIRED MEASUREMENT (follow-up, 2026-10-08): the previous evaluator timed the whole reference suite, then the baseline, then the candidate, and compared best-of-two times; a byte-different copy of the reference beat the reference on every workload in one of two local runs. Both timing metrics now use interleaved paired measurement: four repetitions (repetitions outer, workloads inner), each running one fresh reference and one fresh candidate process back to back in the pre-recorded strict alternation PAIR_ORDER, comparing medians with the unchanged strict C < R and zero tolerance. Strict alternation over an even count keeps both the mean and the median position-balanced under monotone drift. The continuous score keeps its definition (sum over workloads of the lower of the candidate's first two fresh repetitions, against the unchanged sequential best-of-two per-leaf baseline); correctness is now checked on all four candidate and reference repetitions. A byte-identical reference submission still reuses the reference samples. PAPER SETTING (2026-10-11): the earlier statements in this comment that workload profiles, seeds and the timing interval are unchanged describe the revisions they are dated with. This revision keeps the three metrics, the strict per-workload conjunction, the paired schedule, the baseline, the reference patch and the continuous score, and changes the setting. (1) Fact tables are no longer 25,000-70,000 rows drawn with replacement from the 10,000-row sample: each workload is a slice of real Corporacion Favorita sales rows (public copy github.com/bgautijonsson/groceries@f79ac95b1c61ca9767f4e7d379bc2229fd8938fc, train_set_2017.csv.7z, sha256 86276d82a921ac0415d95a776dcf5122b17ed03a58eb8d72d6f9f09b1eef02a5; that repository carries no licence statement) keyed to the JoinBoost artifact's dimension tables, with the artifact's target formula. Development cases have 2,054,144 / 1,540,608 / 1,027,072 / 2,054,144 rows dated 2017-02-02..2017-04-30; graded cases 2,142,914 / 1,607,195 / 1,071,466 / 2,142,929 rows dated 2017-05-01..2017-07-30; depth, estimators, learning rate and topology per profile are unchanged; there are no seeds any more. Every fact row is a distinct item x store-day, so duplicate-row collapsing has nothing to collapse. (2) src/joinboost/executor.py is trusted and byte-locked; it returns at most 10,000 rows per query and 250,000 rows per fit to Python (measured maximum of the reference and of the per-leaf baseline: 6 rows per query, 2,878 and 2,968 rows per fit) and accepts only data statements; DuckDB runs with threads=2 and memory_limit=10GB, external access disabled and configuration locked. Violations are invalid submissions with closed reasons. (3) The sorted-prediction L1 bound is per row (rows * 1e-6): the absolute sum grows with the fact table and the reference's own floating-point noise measured up to 1.3e-8 per row on these workloads, at the old bound's per-row level of 1.4e-8. (4) The materialized-join oracle is fitted once per case in an untimed process; the timed interval is unchanged. Measured with both guards on the authoring host (AMD EPYC 7R13, two pinned cores, 2026-10-11, development suite, six evaluations running concurrently): reference median fit 5.8-6.0 / 8.8-9.1 / 13.5-13.9 / 9.2-9.3 s; residual update including the trusted read 0.60-0.63 / 0.50-0.51 / 0.62-0.63 / 0.86-0.88 s, i.e. about 10.5% / 5.6% / 4.5% / 9.4% of the fit (previously 1-3%); per-leaf baseline total 38.7-40.1 s. A byte-different copy of the reference measured fit ratios 0.936-1.031 and update ratios 0.998-1.019 per workload over two evaluations and cleared 7 and 6 of 8 timing cells, never all, so the strict rule's noise level is a few percent and a chance pass of an equivalent implementation is not excluded. Not measured: the graded suite, the published images, and the platform's own 2-vCPU 16 GiB containers. GUARDS (2026-10-11, same revision): (a) the residual-update interval now includes one trusted full read of the updated target state per round, with a consistency value, so a lazy view or a Python-side pending update no longer yields a near-zero update time: a view is computed in full inside the clock, and a state whose residual column is not yet updated leaves the metric unmeasured. The earlier 'Residual limitation' note is superseded: what remains is that a submission may still move work other than producing the updated residual column (for example dropping superseded tables, or rebuilding auxiliary structures) out of _update_error; that work counts in the conjoined complete-fit time only. (b) A fit that leaves, at any per-round or final check, a relation with at least 10% of the fact rows and more than 9 columns (the fact table's 5 plus 4) is invalid: 'submission materialised the join into a fact-scale relation'. Measured maxima of fact-scale relation width: 5 columns for the reference and the per-leaf baseline on every development workload; 5 for the replayed in-graph designs and 22 for the replayed join-materialising design on a 200,000-row six-table case. The check costs 13-30 ms per fit and the trusted reads 46-107 ms per fit on the reference and baseline (under 1% of the fit). Not caught: vertical partitioning of a materialised join into several narrow fact-scale tables aligned by row position, and a wide relation created and dropped within one round. DENSIFIED WORKLOADS (2026-10-11, same revision): each suite now has eight workloads instead of four, by measuring each of the four unchanged fact slices under two profiles: the four original ones plus (slice 0, depth 1, 24 rounds, lr 0.5, four-table), (slice 1, depth 2, 20 rounds, lr 0.1, five-table), (slice 2, depth 5, 3 rounds, lr 0.5, six-table) and (slice 3, depth 3, 4 rounds, lr 0.5, six-table). Depth spans 1-5 and round count 3-24; profiles were chosen so the reference stays below 7.7 GB resident without spilling (deeper or longer profiles on the 2-million-row slices reached the 10 GB DuckDB limit and were not used). Data files, dataset selectors, guards, tolerances, the strict rule, the four paired repetitions and the score formula are unchanged; the score now sums over eight workloads. The evaluation timeout is 7,200 s. Measured on the authoring host (two pinned cores per evaluation, 2026-10-11): reference median fit about 6.3 / 9.8 / 14.9 / 9.9 / 7.8 / 13.4 / 15.4 / 7.2 s; residual update share about 10.5% / 5.7% / 4.5% / 9.3% / 21% / 9.7% / 3.4% / 5.5%; per-leaf baseline total 87-90 s; one reference-versus-reference evaluation 1,460-1,466 s wall (2,366 s on cores shared with another job). A byte-different copy of the reference measured fit ratios 0.944-1.094 and update ratios 0.919-1.146 per workload over two evaluations (run concurrently with each other) and cleared 9 and 8 of 16 timing cells. DATA CAP (2026-10-11, same revision, review finding): the row cap counted rows, so one row holding a LIST of 250,001 values passed. The trusted executor now caps data: fetched columns must be scalar (BOOLEAN, integers up to HUGEINT/UHUGEINT, FLOAT, DOUBLE, DECIMAL, VARCHAR; nested types, BLOB, BIT, JSON, ENUM and all others are refused from the result description before fetching), with at most 32 columns, 40,000 values and 200,000 bytes per query, 256 characters per string, and 250,000 rows, 250,000 values and 1,000,000 bytes per fit; database error messages are cut to 256 characters, detached from the original exception and charged. Measured maxima on the eight development workloads for the reference, the per-leaf baseline and the three replayed in-database designs: 6 rows, 6 columns, 36 values and 141 bytes per query, 12 characters per string; 3,043 rows, 8,666 values and 66,332 bytes per fit. What remains reachable by design: up to 1,000,000 bytes of scalar values per fit, about 7% of the smallest fact table's key and residual columns.
